questions.question: Wegener's theory of continental drift was rejected for fifty years. Explain the four categories of evidence he offered, giving one South African example, and state why the theory was nevertheless not accepted.
questions.expected_answer: Wegener offered four categories. The FIT of the coastlines: South America nests into the western bulge of Africa, and the fit improves when continental shelves rather than shorelines are matched. FOSSIL evidence: Mesosaurus, a freshwater reptile unable to cross an ocean, occurs in Karoo rocks in South Africa and in identical rocks in Brazil and Paraguay, while Glossopteris, with seeds too heavy to be wind-blown, grew across five now-separated landmasses. GEOLOGICAL evidence: the Cape Fold Mountains continue, with the same age and folding, as the Sierra de la Ventana in Argentina and into the Ellsworth Mountains of Antarctica. CLIMATIC evidence: the Dwyka tillite at the base of the Karoo Supergroup was dumped by a continental ice sheet in a region that is now hot, and matching glacial deposits with scratch marks radiating from a single centre lie in South America, India and Australia. The theory was rejected because Wegener could not name a mechanism — he had no force capable of moving continents through solid ocean floor, and without an engine the evidence was treated as coincidence.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism that drives plate movement, and explain how the ocean floor provided the proof Wegener lacked.
questions.expected_answer: Heat from radioactive decay and from the earth's formation drives convection currents in the plastic asthenosphere: hot, less dense mantle rock rises, spreads sideways beneath the lithosphere, cools, becomes denser and sinks again, completing a cell that turns a few centimetres per year. The mantle is solid rock flowing plastically, not liquid lava. The lithosphere — crust plus rigid upper mantle, about 100 km thick — is broken into plates that ride this circulation, helped by ridge push, where new elevated crust slides off the ridge under gravity, and slab pull, where a cold dense sinking plate hauls the rest behind it. The ocean floor supplied the proof through sea-floor spreading: the sea floor is youngest at the mid-ocean ridge and grows older toward the continents, and is nowhere older than about 200 million years, while continental rock approaches four billion. Palaeomagnetism clinched it: because the earth's magnetic field reverses periodically and cooling lava locks in the prevailing direction, the ocean floor carries magnetic stripes parallel to the ridge and mirrored symmetrically on both sides.

questions.question: Compare the three types of plate boundary in terms of movement, whether crust is created or destroyed, the landforms produced and the associated hazards. Use named examples.
questions.expected_answer: DIVERGENT (constructive): plates move apart and new crust is created. Under the ocean this builds a mid-ocean ridge with a rift groove along its crest, fissure eruptions of runny basaltic lava and shield volcanoes — Iceland and Tristan da Cunha stand above sea level on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. On a continent it builds a rift valley: the East African Rift, where a strip of crust has dropped between parallel faults to leave a flat floor walled by steep scarps, with long deep lakes such as Tanganyika and Malawi and volcanoes such as Kilimanjaro. Earthquakes are frequent but shallow and moderate. CONVERGENT (destructive): plates move together and lithosphere is consumed. Oceanic against continental gives a trench, fold mountains and composite volcanoes — the Nazca plate under South America built the Peru-Chile Trench and the Andes. Oceanic against oceanic gives a trench and an island arc, such as the Mariana Trench and Japan. Continental against continental gives the highest fold mountains, the Himalayas, with powerful earthquakes but no volcanoes because no slab descends to make magma. TRANSFORM (conservative): plates slide past each other and crust is neither made nor destroyed; the San Andreas Fault produces a long straight fault line with features offset sideways, no volcanoes, but severe shallow earthquakes when locked plates finally slip.
